notes.meaning: Early in the morning, the Jewish council held an official meeting to carry out their plan against Jesus. They tied Him up and handed Him over to the Roman governor, Pontius Pilate. Under Roman rule, Jewish leaders did not have the legal right to execute anyone themselves.

Pilate asked Jesus if He claimed to be the King of the Jews, a title that sounded like treason against Rome. Jesus answered, 'You have said so,' agreeing that He was indeed the promised King, but not an earthly rebel seeking political power.
The chief priests poured out many harsh accusations against Jesus before the governor. They acted like public accusers, showing deep anger and hatred toward Him.
Pilate urged Jesus to speak up and defend Himself against this long list of charges. Roman courts expected prisoners to fight for their lives, so the governor wanted Jesus to answer.
Jesus remained completely silent, refusing to argue against false charges. His quiet self-control and dignity left Pilate deeply astonished.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars note that a regular custom of freeing a prisoner at the Passover feast is not recorded outside the New Testament and may have been a local practice used by Pilate.

notes.meaning: Pilate had a habit during the annual Passover feast of setting free one prisoner chosen by the crowd. This practice gave the governor a chance to please the local people.
A rebel named Barabbas was locked in prison with other rioters who had killed someone during an uprising. While Jesus was innocent of treason, Barabbas was truly guilty of violence against Rome.
The crowd came forward and loudly asked Pilate to grant them their usual holiday favor. They demanded that he release a prisoner just as he had done in past years.
Pilate asked the crowd if they wanted him to release Jesus, whom he called the King of the Jews. He hoped the people would choose Jesus and save Him from the priests.
Pilate could see that the religious leaders brought Jesus to trial out of bitter jealousy. Jesus was loved and respected by the people, which made the leaders resent His popularity.
The chief priests moved through the crowd and convinced the people to demand Barabbas instead. Swayed by their leaders, the crowd chose a violent killer over an innocent healer.
Pilate asked what they wanted him to do with Jesus if Barabbas was set free. By repeating the royal title, Pilate highlighted the extreme choice they were making.
The crowd shouted back with one voice, demanding that Jesus be crucified. They called for the most terrible and humiliating death known under Roman law.
Pilate pressed them to name a real crime, asking what evil Jesus had done. Instead of giving an answer, the crowd only screamed louder for His execution.
Pilate chose to please the mob rather than uphold justice, so he set Barabbas free. He ordered Jesus to be severely whipped with a Roman scourge and handed over to be nailed to a cross.
The soldiers took Jesus inside the governor's palace, known as the Praetorium. They gathered the entire company of soldiers stationed there to join in mistreating Him.
The soldiers threw a purple robe over Jesus and twisted sharp thorny branches into a wreath for His head. They used these painful items to parody the fine clothes and royal crown worn by a king.
The soldiers shouted fake royal greetings at Him, calling out, 'Hail, King of the Jews!' They twisted the common pledge of loyalty given to the Roman emperor into an insult against Jesus.
They hit Jesus repeatedly on the head with a wooden staff, drove the thorns into His skin, and spat upon Him. Then they bent their knees in mock worship, laughing at His supposed kingdom.
When the soldiers finished mocking Him, they took off the purple robe and put His own clothes back on Him. Then they marched Him out of the city gates to be executed.

As they walked, the soldiers forced a passerby named Simon from Cyrene to carry the heavy crossbeam for Jesus. Mark names Simon's sons, Alexander and Rufus, because they were well-known believers in the early church.
The soldiers brought Jesus to the execution site called Golgotha, a name that translates to 'The Place of the Skull.' It was a common public spot outside the city where criminals were put to death.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: An ancient Christian tradition holds that Golgotha was the burial site of Adam, which is why Orthodox church art and icons typically depict Adam's skull beneath the feet of the crucified Christ.

notes.meaning: Before nailing Him to the cross, they offered Jesus wine drugged with bitter myrrh to dull His senses and ease the pain. Jesus refused it because He chose to face death fully awake and clear-minded.

The soldiers nailed Jesus to the cross and then threw lots, like rolling dice, to divide His clothing among themselves. While He hung in agony, they treated His few belongings as an executioner's prize, fulfilling ancient prophecy.
